olivia: Heads-up — I have a repro for Mistral long-context memory growth that's different from the usual page-eject noise. Seen it after the 1.23.0 kernel swap on a dedicated pool.

samir: can you paste the minimal repro steps? is this on GQA or MQA builds?

olivia: MQA build. Steps: run 1 session with variable-length prompts (avg 12k tokens) + interleaved short chats. After ~40k tokens memory climbs ~2.2GB over baseline and p99 latency drifts up.

jin: do you have flamegraphs / heapmap?

olivia: yes — attaching a short excerpt:
```
# kv residency sample (trimmed)
step 0: kv_pages=18432, resident=9.8GB
step 40k: kv_pages=21024, resident=12.0GB
GC run: freed 2.7GB but kv_pages still 19876 -> fragmentation high
latency p99: 84ms -> 101ms (+20%)
```

perf-bot: nightly profile flagged regression: kv_realloc_chain events increased x3 since kernel-switch-1.23.0.

reza: "kv_realloc_chain" — interesting name. Pattern?

jin: looked at allocation traces: we get repeated evict->realloc cycles on the same logical slot because rope-scaled attention causes alternating large and small sequences. When a long seq allocates a big contiguous run, subsequent short sequences can't reuse holes because we keep splitting pages with different age tags. Effectively we get a swap-lineage: page A evicted -> page B allocated -> page A reallocated later -> churn.

samir: so fragmentation + frequent partial fills -> higher resident and page-table churn. Any kernel heuristics causing this?

jin: yes. After the kernel swap we now favor the "fast-alloc" path that prefers contiguous runs and defers compaction. That improves pure throughput on steady-state batches but is bad for variable-length workloads like our MQA tests.

olivia: repro also shows that batching heuristic exacerbates it. When batcher packs many short requests onto a worker after a long-one, KV gets a mix of big/small allocations leading to the chain.

reza: did you try toggling compaction on eviction or lowering the eviction aggressiveness?

olivia: quick experiments:
- eviction_threshold 0.7 -> 0.85: reduces resident by ~600MB but increases latency jitter (more immediate evicts).
- force_compact_on_evict=true: frees ~1.9GB but adds ~6% CPU overhead and a small p95 latency bump.

samir: numbers sound useful. Could we instead change kernel selection rule: if model==mistral && rope_scale>1.2 && batch_stddev>some threshold -> pick compacting allocator kernel?

jin: I ran a local patch, kernel-selection rule like that avoids the realloc_chain x3 growth; resident stabilized and p99 returned close to baseline. No obvious regression for steady large-batch tests.

perf-bot: ablation run: compact-kernel policy reduced kv_realloc_chain by 78% and freed 1.7GB average on MQA repro. Overall throughput delta -1.8% for steady logits-only benchmarks.

reza: that seems acceptable if we can toggle by model/telemetry. Also we should consider an adaptive batcher change: prefer packing homogenous seq-lens per worker when variance detected. That reduces mixed allocation patterns.

olivia: agree. Proposed action items:
1) roll the compact-kernel selection rule behind an opt-in flag for the next canary (olivia will add).
2) add batcher telemetry to emit batch_stddev and seq_len_hist per route (jin will prototype).
3) add a lightweight compaction call that runs only when fragmentation ratio > 0.25 and every N tokens (reza will benchmark N).
4) add unit/integration test in perf suite that simulates alternating long/short sequences to prevent regressions.

samir: timeline?

olivia: I'll open a PR with the kernel toggle + harness by EOD tomorrow. Jin will push a batcher telemetry spike next week. Reza will run N sweep and report numbers.

jin: one more note — Llama/GQA runs don't show this to the same extent because their rope scaling is less variable and alloc patterns are more uniform. So targeting Mistral/MQA first makes sense.

reza: sounds good. Also tag eng-sre for canary routing if we flip on canary in prod.

olivia: thanks everyone :thumbsup: I'll dump the repro script and flamegraphs in the ticket and link here.
